lessons.fire-triangle:
**The Fire Triangle — OSHA 29 CFR 1910.39**

Every fire requires three elements to start and continue burning: heat, fuel, and oxygen. Together these form the fire triangle. Heat provides the energy needed to raise a material to its ignition temperature. Fuel is any combustible material — wood, paper, fabric, flammable liquids, gases, or even certain metals. Oxygen, which makes up about 21% of the air we breathe, supports the chemical reaction that sustains combustion.

The fire triangle is not just a concept — it is a practical tool for fire prevention and suppression. Removing any one of the three sides will stop a fire. Water cools a fire by removing heat. Carbon dioxide and dry chemical agents displace oxygen. Cutting off fuel supply — shutting off a gas valve, removing combustible materials — eliminates the fuel source. Fire suppression systems, extinguishing agents, and fire prevention controls all work by attacking one or more sides of the triangle.

Fire prevention means preventing the triangle from completing. Controlling ignition sources keeps heat away from fuel. Proper storage keeps flammable materials away from heat sources. Good ventilation management prevents vapor accumulation near oxygen. Understanding the fire triangle gives every employee a foundation for recognizing fire risk and taking meaningful preventive action.
lessons.flammables-combustibles:
**Flashpoints, Flammables, and Combustibles — OSHA 29 CFR 1910 Subpart H**

A flashpoint is the lowest temperature at which a liquid gives off enough vapor to ignite when exposed to an ignition source. It does not mean the liquid itself burns — it means the vapors above the liquid's surface can ignite. Flammable liquids have flashpoints below 100°F (38°C), which means they can produce ignitable vapors at or near room temperature. Combustible liquids have flashpoints at or above 100°F and are generally less immediately dangerous but still require careful handling.

Common workplace flammable liquids include gasoline, acetone, alcohol, paint thinner, and many solvents. These materials must be stored in approved containers, kept away from ignition sources, handled in ventilated areas, and dispensed in controlled quantities. Safety data sheets (SDS) provide flashpoint information and safe handling guidance for every hazardous chemical — employees should consult the SDS before working with unfamiliar materials.

Vapors from flammable liquids are often heavier than air and can travel along floors, collect in low-lying areas, or accumulate in confined spaces — far from where the liquid was used. This makes vapor control a critical part of flammable liquid safety. Never use flammable liquids near open flames, hot surfaces, or sparking equipment. Keep containers closed when not in use and return excess materials to approved storage.
lessons.fire-classes:
**Classes of Fire and Extinguishing Agents — OSHA 29 CFR 1910.157**

Fires are classified by the type of fuel involved, and the correct extinguishing agent depends entirely on the fire class. Using the wrong agent can be ineffective or can make the fire significantly worse. There are five recognized fire classes in the United States: Class A (ordinary combustibles — wood, paper, fabric, rubber, plastics), Class B (flammable and combustible liquids and gases), Class C (energized electrical equipment), Class D (combustible metals such as magnesium, titanium, or sodium), and Class K (cooking oils and fats, typically in commercial kitchens).

Water is effective on Class A fires but must never be used on Class B fires — it scatters burning liquid and spreads the fire. Water must never be used on Class C fires — it conducts electricity and can cause electrocution. Class D fires require specialized dry powder agents matched to the specific metal. Class K fires require wet chemical agents designed for high-temperature cooking oils.

Every employee who may encounter a fire should know which extinguisher types are present in their work area and which fire classes each is rated for. This information is printed on the extinguisher label. Before attempting to fight any fire, employees must ensure: they are trained to use the extinguisher, the fire is small and contained, their escape route is clear, and the extinguisher matches the fire class. If any of these conditions are not met, evacuate immediately.
lessons.extinguishers:
**Fire Extinguishers and the P.A.S.S. Method — OSHA 29 CFR 1910.157**

Portable fire extinguishers are the first line of defense for small, incipient-stage fires. OSHA requires employers to provide fire extinguishers appropriate to the hazards in the workplace, maintain them in working condition, and train employees in their use. Employees must be trained annually on the general principles of extinguisher use and the hazards of incipient-stage firefighting.

The P.A.S.S. method is the standard technique for using a portable fire extinguisher. Pull the pin at the top of the extinguisher — this unlocks the handle and allows the agent to discharge. Aim the nozzle or hose at the base of the fire, not at the flames. Squeeze the handle to release the extinguishing agent. Sweep the nozzle from side to side at the base of the fire until it is out, working from the edge toward the center.

Before using any extinguisher, verify it is rated for the class of fire you are fighting. Know the location of all extinguishers in your work area and confirm they have been inspected. Do not attempt to fight a fire if it has grown beyond an incipient stage, if you do not have a clear escape route behind you, if you are not confident in your ability to operate the extinguisher, or if the fire involves hazardous materials that require specialized response. When in doubt, evacuate and let trained emergency responders handle it.
lessons.ignition-sources:
**Static Electricity and Hidden Ignition Sources — OSHA 29 CFR 1910 Subpart H**

Ignition sources are not always as visible as open flames or sparks from grinding. Static electricity is one of the most common hidden ignition sources in workplaces that handle flammable liquids and gases. Static charge builds up when materials move against each other — liquid flowing through a pipe, liquid being poured or pumped into a container, or even a person walking across a non-conductive floor. When that charge discharges as a spark near flammable vapors, it can cause a fire or explosion.

Grounding and bonding are the primary controls for static electricity during flammable liquid transfer. Bonding involves connecting two containers together with a conductive wire so they reach the same electrical potential, eliminating the voltage difference that causes sparks. Grounding connects the container to the earth, providing a path for static charge to dissipate safely. Both controls must be in place before liquid transfer begins.

Other hidden ignition sources include friction heat from slipping belts or bearings, overheated electrical components, pilot lights, hot surfaces, and sparks from tools or equipment in areas where flammable vapors may be present. Any ignition source in a flammable atmosphere is a fire risk. Employees should report overheating equipment, ensure no ignition sources are active in flammable vapor areas, and follow area classification rules for electrical equipment used near flammable materials.
lessons.hot-work-hazards:
**Hot Work, Welding, and Combustible Controls — OSHA 29 CFR 1910.252**

Hot work refers to any operation that produces sparks, open flames, or heat sufficient to ignite nearby combustibles. This includes welding, cutting, brazing, grinding, and soldering. Hot work is one of the leading causes of industrial fires because sparks can travel significant distances, penetrate small openings, and ignite materials that appear to be safely out of the work zone.

A hot work permit system is the standard control for managing hot work hazards. Before hot work begins, the area is inspected for combustible materials, the permit documents the hazard controls in place, and a fire watch is assigned to monitor the area during and after the work. Combustibles within the hot work area should be removed or relocated whenever possible. When materials cannot be moved, they must be covered or shielded with fire-resistant blankets, curtains, or shields to prevent ignition.

Fire watches must remain in the area during hot work and for a minimum of 30 minutes after work is complete — many fires start from smoldering materials that ignite after the welder has left the area. Employees performing hot work must be trained in the permit system, hazard recognition, and fire response procedures. Hot work should never be performed without a permit in areas where flammable materials or vapors may be present.
lessons.emergency-response:
**Fire Alarms, Evacuation, and Emergency First Aid — OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38**

When a fire alarm activates, the immediate and correct response is to evacuate according to the Emergency Action Plan — not to investigate, not to collect belongings, not to wait for confirmation. Seconds matter in a fire. Smoke inhalation incapacitates faster than the fire itself, and exits that are clear at the moment the alarm sounds may become blocked within minutes.

During evacuation, feel doors before opening them. If a door handle or door surface is hot, fire is likely burning on the other side. Do not open it — heat and flames can flash through instantly. Find an alternate route, close doors behind you as you go (closed doors significantly slow the spread of fire and smoke), and proceed to the designated assembly area. Do not use elevators during a fire. If smoke is in the corridor, stay low where air is cleaner and move quickly to the nearest exit.

If clothing catches fire, the correct response is stop, drop, and roll. Running feeds oxygen to the flames and makes them worse. Dropping to the ground prevents flames from reaching the face. Rolling smothers the fire by cutting off its oxygen supply. After the flames are out, cool the burned area with cool (not ice cold) water for several minutes and seek medical attention. Do not apply butter, oil, or home remedies to burns. For fires involving others, a fire blanket or CO2 extinguisher can be used to smother flames — never use a dry chemical extinguisher directly on a person.
